4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency, the disease caused by germline *ALDH5A1* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ssadh_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *ALDH5A1* variant or a diagnosis of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *ALDH5A1* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *ALDH5A1* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)

135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;

143

8	# Clinical diagnosis and mutation analysis of four Chinese families with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	BackgroundSuccinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessively-inherited defect of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism. The absence of SSADH, which is encoded by aldehyde dehydrogenase family 5 member A1 (ALDH5A1) gene, leads to the accumulation of GABA and γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB). Few cases with SSADH deficiency were reported in China.Case presentationIn this study, four Chinese patients were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital. We conducted a multidimensional analysis with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, semi quantitative detection of urine organic acid using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and analysis of ALDH5A1 gene mutations.Two of the patients were admitted to the hospital due to convulsions, and all patients were associated with developmental delay. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed the background activity of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. Urine organic acid analysis revealed elevated GHB in all the patients. Mutational analysis, which was performed by sequencing the 10 exons and flanking the intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene for all the patients, revealed mutations at five sites. Two cases had homozygous mutations with c.1529C > T and c.800 T > G respectively, whereas the remaining two had different compound heterozygous mutations including c.527G > A/c.691G > A and c.1344-2delA/c.1529C > T. Although these four mutations have been described previously, the homozygous mutation of c.800 T > G in ALDH5A1 gene is a novel discovery.ConclusionSSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. We describe a novel mutation p.V267G (c.800 T > G) located in the NAD binding domain, which is possibly crucial for this disease’s severity. Our study expands the mutation spectrum of ALDH5A1 and highlights the importance of molecular genetic evaluation in patients with SSADH deficiency.
13	
14	## Background
15	
16	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH, OMIM: 271980) deficiency, also known as 4-hydroxybutyric aciduria, is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder that affects the degradation of γ-aminobutyric acid [1]. SSADH catalyzes succinic semialdehyde (SSA) to succinic acid (SA) in the final step of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) catabolism. In the absence of SSADH, SSA is converted into γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) and other related metabolites. GHB can be converted to 3-deoxytetronic acid (3DT) or 2-deoxytetronic acid (2DT) via α or β oxidation. GABA and GHB accumulate in the brain, blood, urine, and cerebral spinal fluid. The clinical features of this disease are various and non-specific, including developmental delay, intellectual deficit, hypotonia, ataxia and seizures, and especially language delays [2–4]. Severity ranges from mild impairment to a relentlessly progressive neurodegenerative course with intractable seizures in infancy [5]. GABA_A receptor down regulation was previously reported as one of the pathophysiological mechanisms [2], but current data reveal a surprisingly complex pattern of pathophysiology including oxidative stress parameters and dysregulation of autophagy and mitophagy [1].
17	
18	The gene of ALDH5A1 with a full length of 1605 bp containing 10 exons, located in chromosome 6p22.3, and codes 535 amino acids with the first 47 residues representing the mitochondrial targeting peptide [4, 6]. The monomeric SSADH consisted of three domains: an oligomerization domain (174–195 and 525–535), a catalytic domain (308–508), and an N-terminal NAD-binding domain (residues 48–173, 196–307, and 509–524) that is responsible for the binding of NAD^+ to the enzyme [7]. To date, more than 56 mutations of ALDH5A1 have been identified [8] and are considered as the main cause for the decrease or elimination of SSADH activity.
19	
20	Only a few cases of SSADH deficiency have been reported in mainland China [9–12]. In this study, we summarized the characteristics of clinical data and analyzed ALDH5A1 gene mutations in four Chinese patients with SSADH deficiency diagnosed in our hospital. We present a novel mutation (c.800 T > G) in ALDH5A1, which enriches the analysis of ALDH5A1 mutation spectrum. Based on our correlation analysis between SSADH protein function and the clinical data of patients, we speculate that the mutation in NAD binding domain (p.S510F and p.V267G) is crucial for this disease’s severity.
21	
22	## Case presentation
23	
24	Four Chinese patients (two males and two females) at the age of 86 days to 5 years were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital in China from June 2012 to September 2016. These patients had no family history. Detailed data are shown in Table 1. Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electroencephalogram (EEG), and routine tests were conducted. Semi-quantitative analysis of organic acids in urine was performed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), and the results were included in Table 2. Genetic analysis was performed using blood samples collected from the patients and their parents. One hundred healthy children were enrolled as the control group. DNA was extracted by gDNA Mini Kit (BIOMIGA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR amplification for 10 exons and flanking intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene was performed, whose primers and reaction condition were designed based on relevant references [12]. PCR products were electrophoresed on 2% agarose gels and sequenced by biological company (GENEWIZ, Tianjin). The sequencing results were compared with the reference sequence of ALDH5A1 (NM_170740) of NCBI.

59	
60	### Patient 1
61	
62	Patient 1 was a 3-year-old female born at term by cesarean delivery with the history of aspiration of amniotic fluid and was not awaked easily for one day after birth. She was admitted to the hospital due to cough for 5 days and intermittent convulsions for 3 days. She had partial convulsions without fever while awake, she slept after remission, most convulsions were less than two minutes in duration. She had no movement or language disorders during the postictal period. She also presented with developmental delay, especially language delay. Cerebral MRI displayed symmetrical hyperintensity of bilateral basal ganglia and globus pallidus on T2-weighted image (T2WI) and hyperintensity of the bilateral parietal lobe white matter on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging. EEG revealed high voltage of delta and theta wave at approximately 2–4 Hz. Urinary organic acid analysis showed elevated GHB concentrations.
63	
64	Molecular analysis of ALDH5A1 confirmed a compound heterozygous mutation of c.527G > A/c.691G > A (p.G176E/p.E231K) in exons 3 and 4. c.527G > A was inherited from her mother, whereas c.691G > A was inherited from her father. We have previously reported these two mutations [8, 12]. Bioinformatics analysis indicated that p.G176 and p.E231 are highly conserved among species. These mutations were predicted to be “Probably damaging” and “Possibly damaging” based on the Polyphen2 software.
65	
66	### Patient 2
67	
68	Patient 2 is an 86-day-old male conceived through in vitro fertilization and born at 37 weeks by cesarean section due to cord around the neck. His mother had an abnormal reproductive history. Her first baby died of convulsion at 23 days after birth, while her second pregnancy was ectopic. This patient was referred to the hospital due to intermittent convulsions for more than 2 months and exacerbation for 2 days. Partial convulsions occurred while he was awake or asleep without fever. He was back to normal without movement disorders. He presented with decreased attention, poor head control, and thumb abduction. Cerebral MRI revealed patchy hyperintensity in bilateral frontal and parietal lobe on T2WI. Widened ventricle and the interval outside the cerebral were also noted in the cerebral MRI. EEG showed sleep spindle asynchrony. Blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis. GHB in urine was significantly elevated according to urinary organic acid analysis. Unfortunately, this patient died of pneumonia despite rescue efforts.
69	
70	A homozygous mutation variant, c.1529C > T (p.S510F), was identified in exon 10 of the ALDH5A1 gene in this patient. Subsequent targeted mutational analysis of exon 10 of his mother confirmed the segregation of the variant. The healthy father did not carry the sequence variant. p.S510 is highly conserved, its mutation is predicted to be “Probably damaging.”
71	
72	### Patient 3
73	
74	Patient 3 was a 5-year-old boy born at full term with the history of hypoxia after birth. He was admitted to the hospital due to developmental delay complicated with lack of sleep. Urinary organic acid analysis showed a high level of GHB. EEG and cerebral MRI were unclear because both were performed by other hospitals.
75	
76	This patient harbored a novel homozygous mutation of c.800 T > G (p.V267G) in exon 5, which he inherited from his parents. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that p.V267 is highly conserved among species. The mutation was predicted to be “probably damaging” and “disease causing” with a score of approximately equal to 1.
77	
78	### Patient 4
79	
80	Patient 4 was an 8-month-old girl born at full term by natural delivery and referred to the hospital because of developmental delay. The clinical manifestations showed slow pupillary light reflex and hyporeflexia and hypotonia of all limbs. Cerebral MRI revealed widened ventricle, cistern, and sulci, which was considered as delayed myelination (Fig.1). EEG was normal. Urinary organic acid analysis showed an increased excretion of GHB.

86	## Discussion and conclusion
87	
88	SSADH deficiency is a rare inherited metabolic disease characterized by the metabolic disorder of GABA. The incidence rate is unknown but has been estimated at 1:100000 [1]. The first case was reported by Jakobs in 1981 [13]_. Parental consanguinity has been reported in approximately 40% of affected population [9]. The median age at diagnosis of SSADH is 2 years old, but underdiagnosis is suspected [14]. Nearly 80% of patients are diagnosed at the age of 5 years, although a few ones are confirmed in late childhood or adolescence [14], and sporadic patients are diagnosed during adulthood [15]. In this study, patient 3 was born to consanguineous parents. These four Chinese patients were diagnosed at the age range of 86 days to 5 years. The signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency are often non-specific, including developmental delay, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, ataxia, neuropsychiatric problems, and epilepsy. Hypotonia and neuropsychiatric problems each have occurred in 70% of patients, and approximately half of these patients have epilepsy [16]. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, involving disabling obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety in addition to inattention, hyperactive behavior, and sleep disturbances, were also noted [17]. EEG shows generalized spike-waves, photosensitivity discharge, and sleep spindle asynchrony [18]. In this study, patients 1 and 2 presented with convulsions, and all the patients had the history of developmental delay. Patient 4 displayed hypotonia and hyporeflexia. Patient 2 and 4 exhibited decreased attention and sleep disturbances, respectively. EEG showed the background of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. The clinical manifestations of these patients are consistent with the signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency.
89	
90	In this study, we identified four patients with different ALDH5A1 gene mutations. The c.800 T > G (p.V267G) mutation in patient 3 is a novel mutation. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that this mutation was highly conserved across species and might play an important biological role. This mutation was predicted to be “probably damaging” and “disease causing” based on the Polyphen2 software with a score of approximately equal to 1. 267 V is located in the N-terminal NAD-binding domain, the mutation in this domain may influence the combination of SSADH with the NAD^+ molecule.
91	
92	SSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. SSADH activity or molecular genetic analysis of ALDH5A1 gene are used to confirm this disorder [4]. In this study, the GHB in urine was elevated dramatically in these four Chinese patients. Genetic investigation also identified five mutations of ALDH5A1 gene. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle, and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4.
93	
94	In conclusion, we reported five ALDH5A1 gene mutations in four Chinese children with SSADH deficiency. Among these mutations, one novel mutation is presented uniquely in our study. Our study may provide useful information for the gene mutation analysis of ALDH5A1 and contribute to the diagnosis of SSADH deficiency in clinical practices and in the screening of ALDH5A1 gene mutation carriers, especially those undergoing neonatal screening with family histories.

messages.content: 12	BackgroundSuccinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessively-inherited defect of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism. The absence of SSADH, which is encoded by aldehyde dehydrogenase family 5 member A1 (ALDH5A1) gene, leads to the accumulation of GABA and γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB). Few cases with SSADH deficiency were reported in China.Case presentationIn this study, four Chinese patients were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital. We conducted a multidimensional analysis with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, semi quantitative detection of urine organic acid using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and analysis of ALDH5A1 gene mutations.Two of the patients were admitted to the hospital due to convulsions, and all patients were associated with developmental delay. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed the background activity of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. Urine organic acid analysis revealed elevated GHB in all the patients. Mutational analysis, which was performed by sequencing the 10 exons and flanking the intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene for all the patients, revealed mutations at five sites. Two cases had homozygous mutations with c.1529C > T and c.800 T > G respectively, whereas the remaining two had different compound heterozygous mutations including c.527G > A/c.691G > A and c.1344-2delA/c.1529C > T. Although these four mutations have been described previously, the homozygous mutation of c.800 T > G in ALDH5A1 gene is a novel discovery.ConclusionSSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. We describe a novel mutation p.V267G (c.800 T > G) located in the NAD binding domain, which is possibly crucial for this disease’s severity. Our study expands the mutation spectrum of ALDH5A1 and highlights the importance of molecular genetic evaluation in patients with SSADH deficiency.

88	SSADH deficiency is a rare inherited metabolic disease characterized by the metabolic disorder of GABA. The incidence rate is unknown but has been estimated at 1:100000 [1]. The first case was reported by Jakobs in 1981 [13]_. Parental consanguinity has been reported in approximately 40% of affected population [9]. The median age at diagnosis of SSADH is 2 years old, but underdiagnosis is suspected [14]. Nearly 80% of patients are diagnosed at the age of 5 years, although a few ones are confirmed in late childhood or adolescence [14], and sporadic patients are diagnosed during adulthood [15]. In this study, patient 3 was born to consanguineous parents. These four Chinese patients were diagnosed at the age range of 86 days to 5 years. The signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency are often non-specific, including developmental delay, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, ataxia, neuropsychiatric problems, and epilepsy. Hypotonia and neuropsychiatric problems each have occurred in 70% of patients, and approximately half of these patients have epilepsy [16]. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, involving disabling obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety in addition to inattention, hyperactive behavior, and sleep disturbances, were also noted [17]. EEG shows generalized spike-waves, photosensitivity discharge, and sleep spindle asynchrony [18]. In this study, patients 1 and 2 presented with convulsions, and all the patients had the history of developmental delay. Patient 4 displayed hypotonia and hyporeflexia. Patient 2 and 4 exhibited decreased attention and sleep disturbances, respectively. EEG showed the background of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. The clinical manifestations of these patients are consistent with the signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency.

She was admitted to the hospital due to cough for 5 days and intermittent convulsions for 3 days. 68	Patient 2 is an 86-day-old male conceived through in vitro fertilization and born at 37 weeks by cesarean section due to cord around the neck. His mother had an abnormal reproductive history. Her first baby died of convulsion at 23 days after birth, while her second pregnancy was ectopic. This patient was referred to the hospital due to intermittent convulsions for more than 2 months and exacerbation for 2 days. Partial convulsions occurred while he was awake or asleep without fever. He was back to normal without movement disorders. He presented with decreased attention, poor head control, and thumb abduction. Cerebral MRI revealed patchy hyperintensity in bilateral frontal and parietal lobe on T2WI. Widened ventricle and the interval outside the cerebral were also noted in the cerebral MRI. EEG showed sleep spindle asynchrony. Blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis. GHB in urine was significantly elevated according to urinary organic acid analysis. Unfortunately, this patient died of pneumonia despite rescue efforts.

88	SSADH deficiency is a rare inherited metabolic disease characterized by the metabolic disorder of GABA. The incidence rate is unknown but has been estimated at 1:100000 [1]. The first case was reported by Jakobs in 1981 [13]_. Parental consanguinity has been reported in approximately 40% of affected population [9]. The median age at diagnosis of SSADH is 2 years old, but underdiagnosis is suspected [14]. Nearly 80% of patients are diagnosed at the age of 5 years, although a few ones are confirmed in late childhood or adolescence [14], and sporadic patients are diagnosed during adulthood [15]. In this study, patient 3 was born to consanguineous parents. These four Chinese patients were diagnosed at the age range of 86 days to 5 years. The signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency are often non-specific, including developmental delay, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, ataxia, neuropsychiatric problems, and epilepsy. Hypotonia and neuropsychiatric problems each have occurred in 70% of patients, and approximately half of these patients have epilepsy [16]. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, involving disabling obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety in addition to inattention, hyperactive behavior, and sleep disturbances, were also noted [17]. EEG shows generalized spike-waves, photosensitivity discharge, and sleep spindle asynchrony [18]. In this study, patients 1 and 2 presented with convulsions, and all the patients had the history of developmental delay. Patient 4 displayed hypotonia and hyporeflexia. Patient 2 and 4 exhibited decreased attention and sleep disturbances, respectively. EEG showed the background of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. The clinical manifestations of these patients are consistent with the signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency.

8	# Clinical diagnosis and mutation analysis of four Chinese families with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	BackgroundSuccinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessively-inherited defect of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism. The absence of SSADH, which is encoded by aldehyde dehydrogenase family 5 member A1 (ALDH5A1) gene, leads to the accumulation of GABA and γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB). Few cases with SSADH deficiency were reported in China.Case presentationIn this study, four Chinese patients were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital. We conducted a multidimensional analysis with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, semi quantitative detection of urine organic acid using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and analysis of ALDH5A1 gene mutations.Two of the patients were admitted to the hospital due to convulsions, and all patients were associated with developmental delay. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed the background activity of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. Urine organic acid analysis revealed elevated GHB in all the patients. Mutational analysis, which was performed by sequencing the 10 exons and flanking the intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene for all the patients, revealed mutations at five sites. Two cases had homozygous mutations with c.1529C > T and c.800 T > G respectively, whereas the remaining two had different compound heterozygous mutations including c.527G > A/c.691G > A and c.1344-2delA/c.1529C > T. Although these four mutations have been described previously, the homozygous mutation of c.800 T > G in ALDH5A1 gene is a novel discovery.ConclusionSSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. We describe a novel mutation p.V267G (c.800 T > G) located in the NAD binding domain, which is possibly crucial for this disease’s severity. Our study expands the mutation spectrum of ALDH5A1 and highlights the importance of molecular genetic evaluation in patients with SSADH deficiency.
13	
14	## Background
15	
16	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH, OMIM: 271980) deficiency, also known as 4-hydroxybutyric aciduria, is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder that affects the degradation of γ-aminobutyric acid [1]. SSADH catalyzes succinic semialdehyde (SSA) to succinic acid (SA) in the final step of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) catabolism. In the absence of SSADH, SSA is converted into γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) and other related metabolites. GHB can be converted to 3-deoxytetronic acid (3DT) or 2-deoxytetronic acid (2DT) via α or β oxidation. GABA and GHB accumulate in the brain, blood, urine, and cerebral spinal fluid. The clinical features of this disease are various and non-specific, including developmental delay, intellectual deficit, hypotonia, ataxia and seizures, and especially language delays [2–4]. Severity ranges from mild impairment to a relentlessly progressive neurodegenerative course with intractable seizures in infancy [5]. GABA_A receptor down regulation was previously reported as one of the pathophysiological mechanisms [2], but current data reveal a surprisingly complex pattern of pathophysiology including oxidative stress parameters and dysregulation of autophagy and mitophagy [1].
17	
18	The gene of ALDH5A1 with a full length of 1605 bp containing 10 exons, located in chromosome 6p22.3, and codes 535 amino acids with the first 47 residues representing the mitochondrial targeting peptide [4, 6]. The monomeric SSADH consisted of three domains: an oligomerization domain (174–195 and 525–535), a catalytic domain (308–508), and an N-terminal NAD-binding domain (residues 48–173, 196–307, and 509–524) that is responsible for the binding of NAD^+ to the enzyme [7]. To date, more than 56 mutations of ALDH5A1 have been identified [8] and are considered as the main cause for the decrease or elimination of SSADH activity.
19	
20	Only a few cases of SSADH deficiency have been reported in mainland China [9–12]. In this study, we summarized the characteristics of clinical data and analyzed ALDH5A1 gene mutations in four Chinese patients with SSADH deficiency diagnosed in our hospital. We present a novel mutation (c.800 T > G) in ALDH5A1, which enriches the analysis of ALDH5A1 mutation spectrum. Based on our correlation analysis between SSADH protein function and the clinical data of patients, we speculate that the mutation in NAD binding domain (p.S510F and p.V267G) is crucial for this disease’s severity.
21	
22	## Case presentation
23	
24	Four Chinese patients (two males and two females) at the age of 86 days to 5 years were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital in China from June 2012 to September 2016. These patients had no family history. Detailed data are shown in Table 1. Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electroencephalogram (EEG), and routine tests were conducted. Semi-quantitative analysis of organic acids in urine was performed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), and the results were included in Table 2. Genetic analysis was performed using blood samples collected from the patients and their parents. One hundred healthy children were enrolled as the control group. DNA was extracted by gDNA Mini Kit (BIOMIGA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR amplification for 10 exons and flanking intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene was performed, whose primers and reaction condition were designed based on relevant references [12]. PCR products were electrophoresed on 2% agarose gels and sequenced by biological company (GENEWIZ, Tianjin). The sequencing results were compared with the reference sequence of ALDH5A1 (NM_170740) of NCBI.

79	
80	Patient 4 was an 8-month-old girl born at full term by natural delivery and referred to the hospital because of developmental delay. 86	## Discussion and conclusion
87	
88	SSADH deficiency is a rare inherited metabolic disease characterized by the metabolic disorder of GABA. The incidence rate is unknown but has been estimated at 1:100000 [1]. The first case was reported by Jakobs in 1981 [13]_. Parental consanguinity has been reported in approximately 40% of affected population [9]. The median age at diagnosis of SSADH is 2 years old, but underdiagnosis is suspected [14]. Nearly 80% of patients are diagnosed at the age of 5 years, although a few ones are confirmed in late childhood or adolescence [14], and sporadic patients are diagnosed during adulthood [15]. In this study, patient 3 was born to consanguineous parents. These four Chinese patients were diagnosed at the age range of 86 days to 5 years. The signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency are often non-specific, including developmental delay, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, ataxia, neuropsychiatric problems, and epilepsy. Hypotonia and neuropsychiatric problems each have occurred in 70% of patients, and approximately half of these patients have epilepsy [16]. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, involving disabling obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety in addition to inattention, hyperactive behavior, and sleep disturbances, were also noted [17]. EEG shows generalized spike-waves, photosensitivity discharge, and sleep spindle asynchrony [18]. In this study, patients 1 and 2 presented with convulsions, and all the patients had the history of developmental delay. Patient 4 displayed hypotonia and hyporeflexia. Patient 2 and 4 exhibited decreased attention and sleep disturbances, respectively. EEG showed the background of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. The clinical manifestations of these patients are consistent with the signs and symptoms of SSADH deficiency.
89	
90	In this study, we identified four patients with different ALDH5A1 gene mutations. The c.800 T > G (p.V267G) mutation in patient 3 is a novel mutation. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that this mutation was highly conserved across species and might play an important biological role. This mutation was predicted to be “probably damaging” and “disease causing” based on the Polyphen2 software with a score of approximately equal to 1. 267 V is located in the N-terminal NAD-binding domain, the mutation in this domain may influence the combination of SSADH with the NAD^+ molecule.
91	
92	SSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. SSADH activity or molecular genetic analysis of ALDH5A1 gene are used to confirm this disorder [4]. In this study, the GHB in urine was elevated dramatically in these four Chinese patients. Genetic investigation also identified five mutations of ALDH5A1 gene. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle, and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4.
93	
94	In conclusion, we reported five ALDH5A1 gene mutations in four Chinese children with SSADH deficiency. Among these mutations, one novel mutation is presented uniquely in our study. EEG shows generalized spike-waves, photosensitivity discharge, and sleep spindle asynchrony [18]. In this study, patients 1 and 2 presented with convulsions, and all the patients had the history of developmental delay. Patient 4 displayed hypotonia and hyporeflexia. Patient 2 and 4 exhibited decreased attention and sleep disturbances, respectively. EEG showed the background of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. 68	Patient 2 is an 86-day-old male conceived through in vitro fertilization and born at 37 weeks by cesarean section due to cord around the neck. His mother had an abnormal reproductive history. Her first baby died of convulsion at 23 days after birth, while her second pregnancy was ectopic. This patient was referred to the hospital due to intermittent convulsions for more than 2 months and exacerbation for 2 days. Partial convulsions occurred while he was awake or asleep without fever. He was back to normal without movement disorders. He presented with decreased attention, poor head control, and thumb abduction. Cerebral MRI revealed patchy hyperintensity in bilateral frontal and parietal lobe on T2WI. Widened ventricle and the interval outside the cerebral were also noted in the cerebral MRI. EEG showed sleep spindle asynchrony. Blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis. GHB in urine was significantly elevated according to urinary organic acid analysis. Unfortunately, this patient died of pneumonia despite rescue efforts.

12	BackgroundSuccinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessively-inherited defect of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism. The absence of SSADH, which is encoded by aldehyde dehydrogenase family 5 member A1 (ALDH5A1) gene, leads to the accumulation of GABA and γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB). Few cases with SSADH deficiency were reported in China.Case presentationIn this study, four Chinese patients were diagnosed with SSADH deficiency in Tianjin Children’s Hospital. We conducted a multidimensional analysis with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, semi quantitative detection of urine organic acid using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and analysis of ALDH5A1 gene mutations.Two of the patients were admitted to the hospital due to convulsions, and all patients were associated with developmental delay. Cerebral MRI showed symmetrical hyperintense signal of bilateral globus pallidus and basal ganglia in patient 1; hyperintensity of bilateral frontal-parietal lobe, widened ventricle and sulci in patient 2; and widened ventricle and sulci in patient 4. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed the background activity of epilepsy in patient 1 and the disappearance of sleep spindle in patient 2. Urine organic acid analysis revealed elevated GHB in all the patients. Mutational analysis, which was performed by sequencing the 10 exons and flanking the intronic regions of ALDH5A1 gene for all the patients, revealed mutations at five sites. Two cases had homozygous mutations with c.1529C > T and c.800 T > G respectively, whereas the remaining two had different compound heterozygous mutations including c.527G > A/c.691G > A and c.1344-2delA/c.1529C > T. Although these four mutations have been described previously, the homozygous mutation of c.800 T > G in ALDH5A1 gene is a novel discovery.ConclusionSSADH deficiency is diagnosed based on the elevated GHB and 4, 5DHHA by urinary organic acid analysis. We describe a novel mutation p.V267G (c.800 T > G) located in the NAD binding domain, which is possibly crucial for this disease’s severity. Our study expands the mutation spectrum of ALDH5A1 and highlights the importance of molecular genetic evaluation in patients with SSADH deficiency.
64	Molecular analysis of ALDH5A1 confirmed a compound heterozygous mutation of c.527G > A/c.691G > A (p.G176E/p.E231K) in exons 3 and 4. c.527G > A was inherited from her mother, whereas c.691G > A was inherited from her father. We have previously reported these two mutations [8, 12]. Bioinformatics analysis indicated that p.G176 and p.E231 are highly conserved among species. These mutations were predicted to be “Probably damaging” and “Possibly damaging” based on the Polyphen2 software.
